mechanisms.title: Kernel-arbitrated cross-process write ownership
mechanisms.problem: Two processes can write-open the same session log and interleave appends, tearing compressed frames and sequence contiguity; a TTL/rename claim protocol leaves bounded dual-writer races.
triggers: A durable file may be written by more than one process (CLI plus host, SDK plus CLI).
An in-process lock or a claim file is proposed as the only exclusion.
obligations: Take an ownership arbiter outside every writer process: an OS kernel lock held for the whole write-handle lifetime.
Map contention to a typed already-owned error; never wait, retry or steal.
Rely on kernel release on descriptor/handle close (including process death); add no expiry, renewal or takeover bookkeeping.
After acquiring a POSIX lock, verify the locked inode is still the file at the lock path; retry if not.
Acquire when opening an existing artifact for write, or immediately before the first materialization of a new one; a lock-taking handle keeps the lock even if materialization fails.
Release must not delete the lock file, preserving a stable inode for later lockers.
Document platform limits (for example advisory flock on some network filesystems).
steps: Choose the platform primitive (flock on POSIX; named kernel semaphore on Windows with zero filesystem footprint).
Hold it for the write-handle lifetime and map contention.
Expose typed errors to callers; never auto-recover by deleting a live lock.
Test real concurrent processes and crash release.

enforcement.implementation: Kernel lock acquired by the persistence write handle; no writer-side liveness protocol.
enforcement.trust: The kernel, not a writer process, owns liveness and release.
enforcement.failure: Contention fails the second writer with a typed error; a wedged holder blocks that session until exit.
exceptions: Browser-worker deployments stub the lock only because in-process ownership already excludes all writers.

applicability: when: Any multi-process durable writer, especially append-only logs.
exceptions: Single-process-only storage may keep an in-process claim, but must state that boundary.; Network filesystems without reliable locks degrade to in-process exclusion; disclose the limit.
reactivation: If a second writer process becomes possible, the kernel lease is mandatory.

migration.strategy: Replace claim-file/TTL protocols with a kernel primitive per platform.
migration.implementation: Wrap acquisition and release in the write-handle lifecycle; add an identity check and crash test.
migration.requiredSupport: Platform bindings for flock and named semaphores; a typed ownership error.

positive: Two processes contend; exactly one write handle opens; the loser gets the typed already-owned error.
Kill the holder; a successor acquires immediately with no expiry wait.
rejection: Deleting a live lock file does not grant a second writer on POSIX; the design documents that deliberate forfeiture.
recovery: A stale lock file left after release is reusable; the inode identity check passes on the next open.

limitations: Advisory locks are unreliable on some NFS versions.
A live but wedged holder blocks the session until it exits; the source refuses ownership stealing because a revived writer would tear the log.

mechanisms.title: Opt-in concurrency with ordered commits and fail-closed classification
mechanisms.problem: Independent sibling calls add avoidable latency, but naive parallelism makes results, middleware and cancellation order-dependent and lets unproven tools race.
triggers: Several sibling operations are requested together.
A scheduler is tempted to expose concurrency metadata to the model or to hardcode tool names.
obligations: Keep concurrency a host scheduling concern; do not put scheduler policy in model-visible tool metadata.
Require an explicit, synchronous, pure unary opt-in classifier per call; missing, invalid, throwing or non-true results are exclusive.
Treat a true result as a promise that the call may overlap any other true call; relational/resource-conflict rules that the unary contract cannot express remain exclusive.
Only dispatch and the operation body may overlap; pre/post middleware and commit remain in model order.
Commit results and collected context through one cursor in model order, regardless of completion order.
Bound the pool; an exclusive call is a barrier and a pool of one.
On abort, stop replenishment, drain started calls, commit their results in order, record synthetic aborted pairs for undispatched calls.
Keep declarations conservative; a tool without a proven input-sensitive classifier stays exclusive.
A scheduler failure is terminal, not converted into an ordinary result; recover after live dispatches settle and report unknown outcomes honestly.
steps: Add the unary classifier and a tagged execution mode; unknown tools fail closed.
Group consecutive parallel calls; barrier each exclusive call.
Run a rolling pool bounded by a deployment cap; reclassify after barriers and before refills.
Drain and pair aborted calls; preserve the first scheduler failure.

enforcement.implementation: Scheduler groups calls, a rolling pool enforces the cap, and a commit cursor serializes results.
enforcement.trust: The tool's opt-in is a safety promise; the scheduler only checks explicit true.
enforcement.failure: Classifier error or unknown tool means exclusive; scheduler failure stops new dispatches and rethrows after quiescence.
exceptions: A code-execution program owns its own bounded nested pool under the same rules.

applicability: when: Any loop that may execute sibling calls concurrently.
exceptions: Serial execution (cap 1) remains valid and must preserve the same ordering contract.
reactivation: Any new concurrent executor must adopt ordered commit and fail-closed classification.

migration.strategy: Introduce a per-call classifier and an ordered commit cursor before enabling concurrency.
migration.implementation: Start with cap 1; add opt-ins only after a tool proves input-sensitive safety; test reentrancy of wrappers.
migration.requiredSupport: A scheduler with barriers/rolling pool, a model-order commit cursor and synthetic abort records.

positive: Parallel siblings overlap; results and post-context arrive in model order.
An exclusive call drains the current pool and acts as a barrier.
rejection: Unknown tool, invalid arguments, thrown classifier or false returns exclusive.
A registry change between barrier and refill reclassifies the next call as exclusive.
recovery: Abort stops refills, drains started calls, commits ordered results and synthesizes aborted pairs for undispatched calls.
Scheduler failure waits for every started dispatch and rethrows the first error.

limitations: Relational safety (for example non-overlapping writes) cannot be expressed and stays exclusive.
A too-broad opt-in can expose latent shared-state races.

mechanisms.title: Reserve identity before asynchronous creation; adopt-only resume
mechanisms.problem: A create request can time out or be retried, a delayed create can revive a closed resource, and a mistyped resume id can silently open an empty history the caller believes it is continuing.
triggers: A remote create/attach operation is asynchronous and can be retried.
A caller supplies an identity to resume or adopt.
obligations: Let the caller reserve the identity before creation; repeating create with the same live id must not allocate a second resource.
Record a closed id before awaiting allocation so a delayed create cannot revive it.
Persist an unfinished close intent and retry it at startup; only explicit close cleans up, not unmount/teardown signals.
For resume, adopt-only: fail when the persisted object does not exist or when its recorded context (cwd/preset) conflicts; never create on behalf of a supplied id.
Report the minted identity in the first machine-readable event so a supervisor can persist and pass it back.
steps: Mint or accept an id before the request.
Write a pending/closed tombstone before awaiting creation or close.
Deduplicate create on (owner, id); reject or ignore a create after close.
On adopt, validate existence and context, else exit with a diagnostic.

enforcement.implementation: Ids are caller-owned; create is idempotent per id; close tombstones precede awaits; adopt is existence-checked.
enforcement.trust: The host owns allocation and liveness; the client may reserve but not invent state.
enforcement.failure: Duplicate create is a no-op or typed error; adopt of a missing or mismatched target fails rather than creating.
exceptions: A first wake may mint an id because no prior caller exists.

applicability: when: Retryable remote creation, resumable processes, terminals, sessions, jobs.
exceptions: A purely local synchronous factory may skip reservation only if it cannot be retried.
reactivation: Any idempotency or resume feature needs this contract.

migration.strategy: Move identity generation to the caller or the terminal owner and add tombstones.
migration.implementation: Make create idempotent per id, write close intent before await, validate adopt context, and test delayed responses.
migration.requiredSupport: Durable pending-close storage; existence and context checks.

positive: Two create requests with the same owner/id allocate one resource.
A close requested before a delayed create response prevents revival.
rejection: Adopt with an unknown id or mismatched cwd/preset fails with a diagnostic and creates nothing.
recovery: A crash between request and acknowledgement is retried from the persisted close intent; an explicit not-found clears it.

limitations: An id is opaque; validation is limited to non-emptiness and context checks.
A host restart may lose live processes even though layout identity is restored.

mechanisms.title: Publish only a complete staged artifact and retain the previous version
mechanisms.problem: Installing or replacing a managed runtime in place can leave a partially written artifact, and a crash mid-replacement can destroy the only working copy.
triggers: Installing or upgrading a managed payload, plugin, runtime or generated bundle.
An installer or updater writes into a live directory.
obligations: Build and verify the complete payload in a staging location.
Publish by replacement only after staging succeeds; retain the previous directory until the replacement succeeds.
Reuse an installed payload only when its manifest identity matches; reuse must not require reinstalling.
Execute a smoke test against the final payload after temporary files are removed; signature validity alone does not prove the artifact runs.
A development launcher must await preparation so an unfinished build cannot exit successfully.
steps: Stage a complete copy and verify hashes/signatures.
Swap atomically or with a recoverable rename; keep the previous directory.
Run the smoke test on the final path.
Record the signed bytes in the manifest.

enforcement.implementation: Staged copy, atomic replacement, retained previous directory, post-cleanup smoke execution.
enforcement.trust: The installer owns the swap; the smoke test observes the real artifact.
enforcement.failure: A staging or verification failure leaves the old payload usable; a failed replacement keeps the previous directory.
exceptions: A fresh install has no previous directory; it still must not publish a partial stage.

applicability: when: Managed runtimes, plugin bundles, generated release artifacts.
exceptions: Read-only packaged resources may be installed by the platform installer if it provides equivalent atomicity.
reactivation: Any self-updating or managed payload needs staged publication.

migration.strategy: Separate materialization from publication; add a retained previous directory and a final-path smoke test.
migration.implementation: Stage to a temp root, verify, rename, keep the old root, then execute the new artifact once with temp files removed.
migration.requiredSupport: Atomic rename on the target filesystem; a smoke entry point; manifest hashes.

positive: A staged payload replaces the old one only after verification; the old directory survives a simulated failure.
The smoke test runs the final artifact after staging cleanup.
rejection: A hash or signature mismatch aborts before publication and leaves the old payload active.
recovery: A crash after staging but before swap leaves the old payload and a reusable stage; a failed replacement keeps the old directory.

limitations: Running processes can block replacement on Windows.
A cached archive is not proof of completed native preparation.

mechanisms.title: Derive artifact identity from locked inputs, not directory names
mechanisms.problem: A version string or directory name cannot prove which bytes were assembled; two builds with the same label can differ, and a silent assembly change can masquerade as the same artifact.
triggers: Caching, reusing or replacing a built/installed payload.
Multiple release targets or wheel/package sets contribute to one artifact.
obligations: Record application version, top-level tool versions, distribution maps and a digest of locked inputs in a manifest (for example runtime.json), not in the directory name.
Make the digest cover the selected target's archives, shared inputs, distribution versions, tool version and assembly format; unrelated targets must not invalidate it.
Include semantically relevant ordering in the digest and exclude irrelevant ordering; define this explicitly.
Any extraction or assembly change that alters bytes without changing locked inputs requires an explicit format bump.
Normalize package names before duplicate rejection.
steps: Hash the selected target and assembly format.
Write the manifest beside the payload.
Compare manifest identity before reuse; bump the format when the assembler changes.
Keep old manifests readable and distinguishable from current ones.

enforcement.implementation: Current source: scripts/primary-runtime/prepare.ts computes SHA-256 over JSON {format: 7, target, pythonVersion, pythonRelease, nodeVersion (only when pnpm is present), artifact: runtimeLock.targets[target], wheels, pythonPackages, pnpm}. Install metadata validation in tool-workspace-dependencies accepts payloadDigest only as 64 lowercase hex and reuses an installation only when the manifest matches. Source tests cover target isolation, shared-wheel/package-manager invalidation and Python-only identity; they were not executed here. Target adoption remains planned.
enforcement.trust: The manifest is the build's claim; the installer must verify the bytes it consumes.
enforcement.failure: Missing or mismatched identity forces a rebuild or reinstall rather than silent reuse.
exceptions: Legacy manifests without a digest remain readable but are distinguishable from current payloads.

applicability: when: Reproducible builds, caches, managed runtimes, release artifacts.
exceptions: Source-only artifacts may use a commit id if it fully determines bytes.
reactivation: Any reuse decision needs a byte-relevant identity.

migration.strategy: Add a manifest with a canonical input digest and a format version.
migration.implementation: Compute at build time, verify at install time, and test that unrelated targets do not invalidate.
migration.requiredSupport: Canonical serialization and hashing in the build pipeline.

positive: Two builds from the same locked inputs share an identity; a changed archive changes it; a target identity is unchanged by another target's archive.
A shared wheel, a distribution version, the pnpm version, or Python-only omission changes the identity as specified.
rejection: A malformed payloadDigest (not 64 lowercase hex) is rejected at manifest validation.

A changed assembler that keeps format 7 is not detectable by the digest; the change review must reject the missing bump. The inspected source has no automatic assembler-change check, so this is not a runtime rejection guarantee.
recovery: A legacy manifest without a digest is readable but never treated as a current match.

limitations: A digest proves input identity, not runtime correctness.

The format bump is developer discipline: the digest hashes a literal `format` value, so an extraction/assembly change that does not bump it is invisible to the build and installer. Do not claim automatic detection.
Key-order rules are subtle; they must be documented and tested.

mechanisms.title: When a model holds approval authority, fix the policy and fail closed
mechanisms.problem: Delegating approval to a model can let a misclassification execute destructive or exfiltration actions; ad-hoc policy, cached grants or tool-name exemptions remove the safety ceiling.
triggers: A mode lets a model decide whether a tool body may run.
A reviewer or classifier is inserted before execution.
obligations: Define one fixed policy that classifies actual effects, not tool names or claimed intent.
Separate low (allow), medium (allow only with explicit current human/direct-parent authorization naming action, exact target and scope) and high (deny, even if requested).
Treat ambiguous or broader-than-established effects as fail-closed.
Give the reviewer one complete request: fixed policy, environment, project constraints, filtered sourced history and the full pending action (name, description, schema, parsed arguments).
Read the complete action history when authorization identity matters; a bounded window is insufficient.
Exclude untrusted roles (assistant text, tool results, project instructions as authority) from the authority set.
Require exactly one closed-form JSON result with only allowed risk/decision combinations; reject extra fields, other blocks or non-terminal output.
Fail closed on missing step ownership, inconsistent action facts, missing schemas and oversized requests; do not summarize or truncate an authority request.
Review every supported call fresh: no cached grants, no tool-name exemptions, no retries, no second authorization check.
Do not persist reviewer traces or risk labels as durable state.
steps: Build the fixed request partitions from durable facts.
Send one review before the body.
On allow, dispatch immediately; on deny or reviewer failure, stop before dispatch.
On unload, stop new admissions, migrate live sessions to a safe mode, abort and drain reviews.

enforcement.implementation: A pre-dispatch reviewer call with a closed result schema; only allow dispatches.
enforcement.trust: An LLM classifier is not a deterministic security boundary; the fixed ceiling and fail-closed paths are the guarantee.
enforcement.failure: Reviewer failure or invalid output denies the call and reports the specific error; the body never runs.
exceptions: An explicitly installed experimental layer may be absent; then the mode does not exist.
Child/subagent sessions may pin a stricter policy.

applicability: when: Model-mediated approval, auto-approval or risk classification before an effect.
exceptions: A purely advisory label that cannot gate execution is not this mechanism.
reactivation: Any execution gate driven by a model needs the fixed policy and closed schema.

migration.strategy: Ship the reviewer as an explicit opt-in layer with a fixed policy and a closed result schema.
migration.implementation: Build the five request partitions, strict parsing, pre-dispatch enrollment and lifecycle cancellation; test denial, malformed output and oversized requests.
migration.requiredSupport: A pre-execute hook, durable action history, request-header schema, cancellation lifecycle.

positive: A low-risk project-local action is allowed and executes.
A medium action with explicit current human authorization naming target and scope is allowed.
rejection: High-risk exfiltration is denied even when explicitly requested.
Extra JSON fields, duplicate members, wrong block types, missing step ownership and oversized requests all deny without executing.
recovery: A reviewer failure reports its actual cause and denies; unload aborts late allows before dispatch.

limitations: Model latency and token cost.
Misclassification remains possible; filtering untrusted roles does not make the classifier a security boundary.
A PTC program's outer transport and direct node effects are outside the per-call guarantee.

mechanisms.title: A denial always stops the body; approval prompts come after other gates
mechanisms.problem: A late allow, a swallowed denial or a prompt issued before downstream gates can execute a body that policy or another listener rejected.
triggers: A review/approval decision is asynchronous.
More than one pre-execute listener can deny or cancel.
obligations: Enrollment and active-review registration happen synchronously before the first await.
After provider settlement, a lifecycle abort produces a canonical pre-dispatch cancellation even for a late allow, deny or failure.
Caller cancellation keeps runtime priority: a late allow cancels before dispatch; a late failure or final denial keeps that outcome.
Ask a human only after later pre-execute listeners allow the call, so a downstream denial or cancellation wins without prompting.
A final denial must not run the body; expose only a stable denial identity and a not-executed output line, not the input body.
Catching a denial inside a program does not elevate it to an outer failure.
steps: Let all listeners run in order.
If policy says ask and the call is otherwise allowed, request approval.
Dispatch only on allowed-once; on rejection/cancel/unavailable, do not run.

enforcement.implementation: A single dispatch gate after listeners and approval; denial paths return without invoking the body.
enforcement.trust: The runtime owns the body-invocation fact; no caller can claim execution.
enforcement.failure: Deny/cancel/unavailable all mean no execution; the model receives an ordinary failure message.
exceptions: A child may pin never and keep a structured final denial.

applicability: when: Any asynchronous approval or review before an effect.
exceptions: Synchronous validation before any await may reject earlier, but must not bypass later listeners.
reactivation: Any new gate must preserve the no-body-on-deny invariant.

migration.strategy: Centralize dispatch behind one gate and test late-allow races.
migration.implementation: Enroll before await, order listeners, ask after them, and abort on teardown.
migration.requiredSupport: A cancellation-aware tool runtime and approval service.

positive: A denied call produces a structured denial and no body execution.
A later listener denial prevents an approval prompt.
rejection: A late allow after lifecycle abort is cancelled before dispatch.
A late denial under ask yields a cancelled approval and no dispatch.
recovery: Unload aborts and drains reviews; already-started bodies settle under normal cancellation rules.

limitations: A body that starts before a later gate cannot be recalled; gates must precede dispatch.
Some transports (outer code execution) may be outside the per-call guarantee.

mechanisms.title: Fail closed on unknown, invalid or ambiguous classification
mechanisms.problem: Optimistic defaults on unknown tools, invalid arguments, unmapped provider paths or failed native calls turn uncertainty into authority.
triggers: A policy decision depends on a classifier, registry lookup or capability probe.
A native call or provider mapping can fail.
obligations: Only an explicit positive opt-in enables the less restrictive path; unknown tools, invalid arguments, thrown classifiers and other return values take the restrictive path.
Validate arguments before invoking a typed classifier; invalid arguments classify restrictive and surface the ordinary argument error only if the call executes.
Do not create a parallel allowlist where an existing composed capability already defines access; derive policy from that capability.
Reject missing/unmapped provider paths instead of substituting a same-named local object.
Every native call failure is fail-closed; record the error rather than continuing with a partial effect.
An idempotent skip must require the exact full precondition (for example exact allow ACE, exact deny ACE and exact label), not a subset.
steps: On any error/absence, take the restrictive branch.

enforcement.implementation: Restrictive branch is the default in the scheduler, access policy and native helpers.
enforcement.trust: The decision owner resolves facts; callers cannot assert safety.
enforcement.failure: Unknown/invalid means deny or exclusive; a native error aborts the effect.
exceptions: A documented, tested capability may be treated as safe only when the source states that exact condition.

applicability: when: Concurrency opt-in, access control, native operations, provider mapping.
exceptions: Purely diagnostic reads with no effect may degrade to a generic fallback, but must say so.
reactivation: Any new classifier needs the same default.

migration.strategy: Invert defaults: absence/error means restrictive.
migration.implementation: Add typed validation, explicit opt-ins, and negative tests for unknown and throwing paths.
migration.requiredSupport: A live registry/capability resolver and typed errors.

positive: An explicit true/declared capability takes the permissive path.
rejection: Unknown tool, invalid args, thrown classifier, unmapped provider path and native error all take the restrictive path.
recovery: After a transient lookup failure, a later successful resolution may take the permissive path; the earlier call is not retroactively allowed.

limitations: A wrong positive declaration is not caught by fail-closed defaults.
Some platform APIs cannot distinguish all failure modes.

mechanisms.title: Delete only what you own; protect shared data and continue past locked items
mechanisms.problem: An uninstaller or cleanup routine that removes shared user data, follows links or aborts on the first locked file either destroys data another product needs or leaves large residue.
triggers: Uninstall, cleanup, cache purge or destructive migration.
Several products share a home directory.
obligations: Delete only the product-owned Electron/user-data and updater caches; never the shared home that holds sessions, credentials, settings and plugins.
Remove empty ordinary parents only; never remove linked or non-empty scope directories.
Reject protected OS directories and paths overlapping the installation or protected home.

Hold directory handles during traversal so paths cannot be renamed/replaced underneath; unlink reparse points without entering targets; clear read-only attributes; keep deleting siblings after a locked file.
Require a fixed local drive; leave a linked root or ancestor untouched.
A failure leaves residue and does not abort the rest or show a custom prompt.
Support an update/keep-data flag; silent uninstall removes the same owned data.
A home path published as an environment variable protects every overlapping target.
steps: Compute owned roots from product identity.
Traverse with handles, no link following.
Report residue; never touch shared home.

enforcement.implementation: A native helper performs deletion with protected-path and overlap checks.
enforcement.trust: The helper, not the UI, enforces ownership.
enforcement.failure: Residue remains; uninstall continues; no data is deleted outside owned roots.
exceptions: An explicit update/keep-data mode retains owned data too.

applicability: when: Destructive cleanup in a shared user environment.
exceptions: A product that owns the entire home may delete it only if it can prove no sibling product uses it; the source rejects profile presence as such proof.
reactivation: Any uninstaller or purge tool needs an ownership boundary.

migration.strategy: Move deletion into a helper with an explicit owned-root allowlist and overlap rejection.
migration.implementation: Add handle pinning, link unlink-not-follow, read-only clearing, sibling continuation, and fixtures for update/keep flags.
migration.requiredSupport: Native filesystem APIs with reparse-point inspection.

positive: Owned Electron data is removed; shared home, sessions and credentials remain.
Update/keep-data mode retains data.
rejection: Protected directories, paths overlapping the install/home, linked roots and network drives are refused or left in place.
recovery: A locked file leaves residue but deletion continues; reinstall restores shared data.

limitations: The native helper cannot see a home configured only in a shell profile.
macOS cleanup is deferred in the source.

mechanisms.title: Every enforcement layer must close a distinct bypass
mechanisms.problem: An access-control layer can appear to confine writes while a second OS authorization path (parent-directory delete rights) bypasses it; adding a layer without naming the bypass it closes creates false assurance.
triggers: A security boundary relies on one OS access check.
A test demonstrates an escape that the existing model cannot express.
obligations: Enumerate every authority path the OS accepts, not just the object's own descriptor.
For each layer, state the exact bypass it closes and why the others cannot.
Keep all layers load-bearing; test removing or narrowing each one.
Narrow inheritance flags to the smallest scope that still closes the bypass (for example container-only deny) and measure the side effects.
Make the standing part of the policy idempotent and independently revocable where grants overlap.
Fail closed on every native call and document the externalities (standing label widening, WRITE_OWNER requirement, denied FullControl opens).
steps: Add the minimal layer that reaches it.
Measure collateral effects on real objects.
Require exact preconditions for idempotent skip.
Test real processes and real tokens, not only synthetic ACLs.

enforcement.implementation: ACL edits (capability allow, parent-delete deny, mandatory label) applied in one call; token lowered to match.
enforcement.trust: The kernel enforces the mandatory policy inside the access check.
enforcement.failure: Any Win32 failure aborts the grant/operation; errors are fail-closed.
exceptions: Read-only modes may use a different integrity level only if the confined shell still starts; the source measured that Untrusted cannot.

applicability: when: OS-level sandboxing or access control with more than one authorization path.
exceptions: A platform with a single enforceable check may need one layer, but must prove there is no second path.
reactivation: Any demonstrated escape reopens the layer analysis.

migration.strategy: Reproduce the bypass in a real environment, add the minimal layer, then test each layer's necessity.
migration.implementation: Apply the three edits atomically, lower the token, require the exact triple for idempotency, and document costs.
migration.requiredSupport: Native ACL APIs and a real confined runner.

positive: Out-of-root deletes are denied through cmd, .NET, Remove-Item and libuv while host files survive.
One granted root cannot delete inside another.
rejection: File-level FullControl opens inside the root still succeed; directory FullControl opens are denied.
recovery: Revoking one of two grants leaves the other usable; a root granted by an earlier build picks up the missing layer on next provision.

limitations: The standing Low label widens the tree for any same-user Low process and outlives the product.
A granted directory must also grant WRITE_OWNER for its label.
FAT-like targets are unverified.

mechanisms.title: Give each trust model its own surface; never substitute across identities
mechanisms.problem: Reusing a document renderer for an arbitrary Web page, or mapping a provider path to a same-named local file, hides a different trust model and can expose data or authority the user did not grant.
triggers: A new content type has different execution, network or identity semantics from an existing viewer.
A remote/provider path is presented as if it were a local path.
obligations: Separate surfaces by trust model (for example document preview versus live Web browsing) instead of overloading one renderer.
Parse addresses against a strict scheme allowlist; reject credentials, the application's own origin, malformed addresses, file: and unknown schemes.
Do not add a host-side probe/proxy for arbitrary targets; it creates an SSRF path and can disagree with later redirects.
Default to a sandbox; any escape is per-occurrence, non-persistent, explicitly warned and never inherited by later tabs.
Honestly model unsupported capabilities (for example unknown cross-origin history) and disable actions the platform cannot support.
Do not auto-activate saved third-party pages; require an explicit restore.
Never substitute a same-named local object for an unmapped provider object.
Keep consent scoped: inherited parent feedback does not authorize a child export.
Do not present process or runner isolation as a security boundary unless it is actually enforced as one; state the limitation instead.
steps: Default-deny capabilities; expose explicit, scoped escape.

enforcement.implementation: Separate tab/renderer type, strict parser, sandbox attribute, no host proxy, explicit restore.
enforcement.trust: The browser/OS carrier enforces isolation; the parser enforces scheme and origin.
enforcement.failure: Invalid addresses and unmapped paths are rejected; unsupported controls are disabled.
exceptions: A per-occurrence sandbox escape may be offered with a persistent warning; it is not persisted.

applicability: when: Embedding third-party content, browsing, remote files, provider paths, consent-scoped export.
exceptions: A surface that only receives pre-selected bytes may use a simpler renderer if it never executes active content.
reactivation: Any new active content type requires a new trust analysis.

migration.strategy: Create a dedicated surface and a strict address parser; keep local-file and Web trust models separate.
migration.implementation: Default sandbox, per-occurrence escape, no host probe, explicit restore, collision-free provider mapping.
migration.requiredSupport: Carrier isolation (iframe/webview), scheme allowlist, user warning UI.

positive: HTTP(S) links open in the browser surface; local files stay in the document preview.
A cross-origin navigation shows an explicit unknown state and disables unsupported history actions.
rejection: file:, credentials, malformed URLs and the app origin are rejected.
A provider path without an identity mapping is rejected; a same-named local file is never opened.
recovery: A saved page is not requested until the user restores it; closing the tab removes its checkpoint only when the authoritative inventory no longer contains it.

limitations: Many sites refuse framing; browser policies (mixed content, private network) remain.
Sandbox escape trades protection for compatibility and can navigate the top-level app.
Persisted URLs may contain sensitive query values.

mechanisms.title: Separate durable state from transient request projections
mechanisms.problem: Using one admitted artifact as both durable history and every later request payload forces one limit to serve incompatible concerns and lets a rejection or optimizer change history.
triggers: An artifact is stored durably and also sent/derived per request.
Different routes, models or budgets impose different projections.
obligations: Keep the durable record provider-independent and normalized; store only a reference in history.
Derive a deterministic per-route request projection (variant identity covers format, dimensions, encoder, quality and all parameters).
Cache derived projections by identity; validate header facts on a hit instead of trusting a key.
Keep inline bytes and provider file ids transient; never rewrite existing history when projections change.
Publish exact totals only when every contributing attempt reported them; otherwise omit the disclosure.
Price or measure under the effective route at measurement time, storing route-neutral facts rather than a precomputed baseline.
steps: Define the durable normalized form and its independent limits.
Project per request; cache by id and verify.
Omit or degrade when evidence is incomplete.

enforcement.implementation: Durable reference plus derived, cached request variants; exactness checks before disclosure.
enforcement.trust: The owner of each route computes its projection; history never depends on it.
enforcement.failure: Missing/corrupt historical attachments remain fail-loud and are reported by attachment identity; durable quarantine and verified recovery are proposed and unimplemented (tracked by .agents/notes/proposed/bug-fix/2026-08-20-attachment-read-quarantine.md). Failed projection falls back to a bounded inline form; incomplete totals produce no disclosure.
exceptions: A route that cannot project may use a text-only substitution, never a guessed visual price.

applicability: when: Media attachments, token accounting, request optimization, any derived view over durable history.
exceptions: A single-route system may compute on demand, but must still keep history independent.
reactivation: Any second route or limit change requires the split.

migration.strategy: Introduce a durable normalized artifact and a versioned per-route projection.
migration.implementation: Store references; add variant ids and verified caches; make disclosures exact-or-absent.
migration.requiredSupport: Content-addressed storage, route adapters, bounded caches.

positive: History keeps one normalized reference across turns; derived variants differ by route without rewriting history.
A complete per-turn total renders; an incomplete one renders no row.
rejection: A cache hit with mismatched header facts is not used.
A text-only route prices substitution text, not phantom visual tokens.
recovery: A malformed cache index is treated as empty; a failed remote lookup falls back to the smaller inline budget.
A missing or corrupt historical attachment fails loudly with its identity; no quarantine or verified recovery is claimed.

limitations: Derived storage consumes additional space.
Encoder/transform changes create new identities without rewriting old history.
Conservative pricing can over-estimate.
Durable quarantine and verified recovery are proposed future work, not current behavior.

mechanisms.title: Publish only committed durable state; ignore discarded attempts
mechanisms.problem: Projecting live deltas, retried attempts or UI state into a durable or machine-readable interface exposes content the log does not contain and makes replay unstable.
triggers: An API/event stream is derived from an agent/session log.
Retries or streaming produce partial attempts.
obligations: Project text/reasoning only from committed messages, never from live attempt deltas; ignore discarded attempts.
Each committed content block becomes exactly one event; do not double-publish a tool call from both a block and its event.
Project tool results only when they append to the surface, not when a compaction replaces older history.
Derive final text and exit status from flushed durable settlements, not from progress-presentation state.
A streaming projection may exist, but must be declared transient and must not feed the durable record.
Replay must fail loudly on malformed durable records and stay failed rather than silently repairing.
steps: Deduplicate ownership between content blocks and events.

enforcement.implementation: Projection filters on committed message/append markers and step ownership.
enforcement.trust: The log is authoritative; the UI is not.
enforcement.failure: Malformed records fail replay; missing step ownership fails closed.
exceptions: A live UI may show pending calls, but not as durable facts.

applicability: when: Event streams, APIs, replay, resume, any derived durable view.
exceptions: A purely ephemeral progress indicator may use live frames if clearly non-durable.
reactivation: Any new projection must name its commit point.

migration.strategy: Identify commit points and filter out deltas/retries.
migration.implementation: Add step ownership, append-only result filtering, and replay tests for discarded attempts.
migration.requiredSupport: A durable log with commit markers and step identity.

positive: A retried step publishes only the committing attempt.
Two consecutive runs with the same id share history and replay identically.
rejection: A discarded attempt's text/reasoning never appears.
A compaction replacement is not emitted as a new tool result.
recovery: A malformed log fails replay with a diagnostic; it does not silently drop or repair records.

limitations: Cold start plus replay grows with session length.
Streaming consumers lose live token-level text.

mechanisms.title: One complete ordering authority; filters are projections, not rewrites
mechanisms.problem: Persisting a filtered or per-view order loses hidden positions; a separate pin sequence creates a second ordering authority and breaks drag behavior.
triggers: A list has visibility filters, grouping, pinning or multiple sort modes.
A UI writes an order back to storage.
obligations: Keep one complete sequence per owner/account, including hidden members; membership bounds it.
Filtering and grouping change display only; never rewrite stored positions.
Supplement missing members in memory and adopt the supplemented sequence only on the next explicit order write.
Make state transitions mutually exclusive in one durable write (for example archive drops the pin).
A pin is an intentional reorder; unpin does not restore a prior slot.
Restoration/removal is idempotent and does not probe existence when removing an id cannot introduce an unknown referent.
Ignore a stale response when a newer request or pushed state supersedes it.
steps: Serialize operations and reject stale replies.

enforcement.implementation: A single stored sequence and derived views; one serialized write path.
enforcement.trust: The registry owns authority; views cannot overwrite hidden positions.
enforcement.failure: A failed write leaves the previous sequence; a stale reply is ignored.
exceptions: A chronological mode may ignore manual positions but still preserves them.

applicability: when: Ordered collections with filters, pins, archives, grouping.
exceptions: A truly stateless sorted view needs no stored sequence.
reactivation: Any second ordering source requires merging or explicit precedence.

migration.strategy: Replace filtered/per-view persistence with one complete sequence and derived views.
migration.implementation: Add supplementation, single-write exclusivity, idempotent removal and stale-reply rejection.
migration.requiredSupport: Optimistic concurrency / revision tokens.

positive: Filtering hides rows without changing their stored positions.
Pinning moves one row to the front of the complete sequence; unpin only clears the mark.
rejection: A drag based on display indices cannot drop hidden members.
Pinning an archived row fails.
recovery: A stale unary reply is superseded by a newer request or pushed increment.
An absent id removal is a no-op with no write.

limitations: An orphan id without a loaded summary has no visible restore row.
Pin timestamps are not used for Last-updated ordering.

mechanisms.title: One ordered state owner; supersede stale replies
mechanisms.problem: Concurrent reads and optimistic writes can apply an older snapshot over a newer one, or let two surfaces disagree about the selected value.
triggers: A client reads state and also applies pushed updates or optimistic writes.
Multiple views can mutate the same selection.
obligations: Have one ordered state owner per account/session; clients render one snapshot from one source, not a merge of partial reads.
Attach ordering (sequence control frames or revisions) to pushed updates; ignore a stale unary reply when a newer pushed increment or request supersedes it.
Use optimistic updates with a defined rejection path: roll back or refetch, never leave the optimistic value silently.
After reconnect or hard reload, obtain a fresh snapshot; never resume from a stale cursor without revalidation.
A local selection change wins until the host confirms or rejects it; then the confirmed state is authoritative.
steps: Read a snapshot and its cursor.
Apply ordered pushes above the cursor.

enforcement.implementation: Sequence/revision checks at the applying store; one snapshot source.
enforcement.trust: The owner's version is authoritative; clients cannot invent ordering.
enforcement.failure: A stale reply is dropped; a gap triggers a full refresh; a rejected optimistic write rolls back.
exceptions: A read-only diagnostic view may lag if it labels the snapshot time.

applicability: when: Live-updated lists, selections, settings, model choice.
exceptions: Files with no concurrent writer may use last-write-wins if documented.
reactivation: Any push channel or optimistic write needs supersession.

migration.strategy: Introduce revision/cursor and a single applying store.
migration.implementation: Tag replies, compare, refetch on gap, roll back rejected optimism.
migration.requiredSupport: Versioned snapshots or sequence control messages.

positive: A pushed update with a higher sequence replaces the local view.
rejection: A late unary reply with an older revision cannot overwrite the newer state.
recovery: A detected gap triggers a fresh snapshot; a rejected optimistic write restores the confirmed value.

limitations: Clock-free sequence requires a single owner; multi-writer state needs a stronger protocol.
Full snapshots can be costly at scale.

mechanisms.title: One explicit owner per resource, card, flow or setting
mechanisms.problem: Two components that each believe they own a card, flow, setting or appearance channel produce duplicate rendering, divergent defaults or one owner clearing another's state.
triggers: A resource can be represented in more than one place.
Multiple plugins can contribute to the same slot.
A setting is read in several components.
obligations: Name exactly one owner for each resource/flow/slot; other contributors add data or intents, never a second representation.
Give one component the whole card/row; subparts are children, not independent tool rows.
Read a setting through one path, once, before dependent surfaces hydrate; do not let each surface define its own default.
A preview or draft read must not mutate the owned state; activation stays with the source owner.
steps: Route all writes through the owner.
Do not let contributors write the owner's state.

enforcement.implementation: Single owner module/store per resource; one settings read path.
enforcement.trust: The owner is a code seam, not a runtime permission.
enforcement.failure: A non-owner write is rejected or ignored; a duplicate owner path is a review defect.
exceptions: A temporary migration may dual-read but must not dual-write.

applicability: when: Cards, dialogs, settings, flows, sockets, appearance, layout slots.
exceptions: Independent resources may each have an owner; this is per resource, not one global owner.
reactivation: Any second writer/representation requires an explicit contract.

migration.strategy: Consolidate duplicate owners into one; convert others to contributors.
migration.implementation: Move writes behind the owner and delete the duplicate path. Adoption guidance (not source-derived): generation-guard releases so a late release from an old holder cannot clear a newer holder's state; when ownership transfers, state the handoff and invalidate the old owner's pending work.
migration.requiredSupport: A stable slot/registry and a settings store.

positive: One card renders per resource even when two contributors supply data.
One settings value applies to every surface.
rejection: A second independent writer is rejected or has no effect.
A second contributor cannot render a second card/tool row; the owner renders subparts as children.
recovery: A rejected owner write leaves the prior state; a remount re-reads the single setting.

limitations: Ownership boundaries need maintenance as features move.
A shared slot can still let contributors render conflicting content if the contract is vague.
Single ownership is source-derived; release-generation and ownership-transfer guards are adoption guidance, not statements in the five cited notes.

mechanisms.title: One geometry/layout authority; surfaces receive slots, not coordinates
mechanisms.problem: Panels that each compute widths, breakpoints or split geometry drift, fight resizing and duplicate constants.
triggers: A multi-pane layout supports docking, resizing, collapsing or floating.
Several components need the same dimensions.
obligations: Keep one normalized layout tree and one engine that computes geometry; surfaces render slots derived from it.
Brand ids and mint them through the engine so no consumer fabricates a node.
Components render a snapshot and report settled intents; gestures preview locally but commit one operation.
Keep one stylesheet for the layout kit; consumers compile sources rather than fork CSS.
Persist layout as the engine's normalized state, not as per-panel pixel copies.
steps: Define the node model and operations.

enforcement.implementation: A dependency-free layout kit owns the tree; panels consume slots.
enforcement.trust: The engine is the only writer of layout state.
enforcement.failure: An invalid operation is rejected; a stale panel snapshot is re-rendered from the engine.
exceptions: A fixed single-pane surface may use static CSS without the engine.

applicability: when: Docking, split panes, resizable columns, floating windows.
exceptions: Truly independent overlays may position themselves if they do not claim layout state.
reactivation: Any second geometry authority requires consolidation.

migration.strategy: Extract geometry into a kit and convert panels to slots.
migration.implementation: Brand ids, snapshot rendering, intent reporting, one stylesheet.
migration.requiredSupport: A normalized tree store and pointer-gesture layer.

positive: A split operation returns the next tree plus its undo operations; `replay(initial, ops)` reproduces the same tree from the same start.
A drag previews locally and commits one settled operation; node ids are branded `PaneId`/`SplitId`/`TabId` and minted only by the engine.
The layout kit keeps exactly one stylesheet; `ui-sidebar-right` stores one `SurfaceState` per session id rather than per-panel pixel copies.
rejection: A panel cannot fabricate a node id or write geometry directly.
recovery: A failed operation leaves the prior tree; replay reads no clock and no random source.

limitations: An engine adds abstraction for simple layouts.
Branded ids and snapshots require discipline in every consumer.

mechanisms.title: Durable artifacts are referenced by stable handles, not copied into every surface
mechanisms.problem: Re-rendering an artifact from a second copy lets the copies disagree; embedding bytes in every message duplicates storage and gives the model stale content.
triggers: A generated artifact (plan, image, file) must survive reloads and appear in several surfaces.
A model request needs the artifact.
obligations: Keep the authoritative artifact once (durable log/attachment store) and reference it by a stable handle/id.
Derived surfaces read the reference; they do not persist a second durable copy.
A preview may be transient and browser-lifetime-scoped; it must not claim durability.
The log owns the exact submitted text/bytes; a rejected invocation may still retain its artifact but must not certify approval.
Provider-side file handles are transient; re-materialize from the durable form when needed.
steps: Write the artifact once and record its handle.
Resolve on render from the store.

enforcement.implementation: Single durable write plus handle references; UI resolves at read time.
enforcement.trust: The store/log is authoritative; the UI cache is disposable.
enforcement.failure: A missing artifact renders an explicit unavailable state; it is not reconstructed by guess.
exceptions: Small inline values may be duplicated if the source states an explicit size bound.

applicability: when: Plans, attachments, generated files, images, long tool outputs.
exceptions: Ephemeral previews with no durability claim may hold their own copy.
reactivation: Any second durable copy needs reconciliation.

migration.strategy: Move artifacts into the store and replace copies with handles.
migration.implementation: Add stable ids, resolve-on-render, transient preview scope, provider re-materialization.
migration.requiredSupport: Content-addressed or log-backed artifact storage.

positive: A plan card survives reload by resolving its logged invocation.
One attachment is stored once and referenced by several turns.
rejection: A preview cannot become a second durable source.
A missing handle shows unavailable rather than re-deriving text.
recovery: A transient provider handle is re-created from the durable artifact; a failed resolution shows an explicit error.

limitations: References create lifetime/GC obligations.
A log-backed artifact may be expensive to read on every render; caching is needed.

mechanisms.title: Stable machine identity, separate human label
mechanisms.problem: Using a display name as the routing key makes identity change with language, rename or collision, and makes persisted references unstable.
triggers: An entity has a user-visible name and is also referenced by tools, storage or routes.
Localization or rename is possible.
obligations: Persist and route by a stable opaque id or a fixed language-neutral key; treat the human name as a projection.
A default stored name is a fixed neutral string; only the on-screen label is localized.
Renaming changes the label, not the identity or existing references.
Reject duplicate names where the name is the identity; otherwise allow duplicates and disambiguate display.
Never infer identity from a basename, path segment or title when an id exists.

enforcement.implementation: Ids in records and APIs; labels computed at the edge.
enforcement.trust: The owner mints ids; consumers cannot derive them from labels.
enforcement.failure: A missing id is an error; a duplicate name is rejected only for name-keyed entities.
exceptions: A user-chosen unique name may serve as the id if rename is forbidden or migrates references.

applicability: when: Workspaces, subagent instances, files, plugins, sessions, models.
exceptions: Purely local display-only values need no id.
reactivation: Any rename or localization feature requires the split.

migration.strategy: Introduce a neutral key, migrate records, and localize labels.
migration.implementation: Keep old localized names as labels; do not rename directories or break references.
migration.requiredSupport: A stable id generator and a display-label function.

positive: Changing the UI language changes the label only; stored keys and paths stay fixed.
rejection: A route or tool call that keys on the label fails or is normalized to the id.
A duplicate name is rejected where identity is name-based.
recovery: Legacy localized names remain readable as labels; no bulk rename is attempted.

limitations: A name that is also an id cannot be renamed without migration.
Display disambiguation may still be ambiguous to users.

mechanisms.title: Show only observed facts; name unknown and unavailable states
mechanisms.problem: A renderer that fills gaps with guesses (a shortened path, a fabricated file, a placeholder preview, a claimed read range) turns absence of evidence into a false statement.
triggers: A UI renders data that may be missing, partial, stale or outside the loaded window.
A summary or coverage artifact is produced.
obligations: Abbreviate or summarize only when the exact precondition holds; otherwise show the full value.
Render an explicit empty/unknown/unsupported state rather than a plausible placeholder.
Never fabricate file paths, coverage ranges or read claims from names or expectations.
Preview content is transient and labeled as such; it is not evidence that the artifact is durable.
A status summary/card derives from durable facts; it does not certify approval or execution that did not happen.
Disclose the exact scope of what was read or inspected; do not imply a full read from a sample.
A derived index refresh must fail closed: an unreadable root or failed refresh leaves prior entries and is retried, never published as an empty replacement.
A discovery label reads projections, not full logs; a missing projection is labeled by id, not backfilled by reading the log.
steps: Check whether the fact is known and in scope.
Render the known value or an explicit unknown state.
Record actual ranges in coverage artifacts.

enforcement.implementation: Explicit conditionals for abbreviation/unknown; evidence fields record real ranges.
enforcement.trust: The UI/summary is not an authority; the underlying record is.
enforcement.failure: Missing data shows unavailable; an out-of-window value is marked, not interpolated.
exceptions: A deliberately approximate label may be shown if marked approximate and bounded.

applicability: when: Path display, previews, coverage reports, inspector, status summaries.
exceptions: Decorative placeholders with no factual claim are acceptable if visually distinct.
reactivation: Any new summarization or coverage claim needs this review.

migration.strategy: Replace guessed fallbacks with explicit unknown states and record actual evidence.
migration.implementation: Add precondition checks, labels, and tests for absent/partial data.
migration.requiredSupport: Source records that can answer in-scope questions.

positive: A home-rooted path shortens only when it exactly matches the home prefix; other paths show full.
A missing preview renders an explicit unavailable state.
rejection: A Windows drive path never becomes ~.
A plan card for a rejected invocation still renders the plan but does not certify approval or execution; a status row without durable evidence shows unavailable.
recovery: A later successful fetch replaces the unknown state; the earlier absence is not retroactively claimed as covered.

limitations: Explicit unknown states add UI surface.
A coverage artifact can still be incomplete; the obligation is to disclose, not to be omniscient.

mechanisms.title: Stable machine-readable codes and event shapes; prose is not an API
mechanisms.problem: Scripts and supervisors parse human prose or incidental field order; a copy or localization change then breaks automation.
triggers: A CLI/API/event stream is consumed by a program.
An error is shown to both humans and machines.
obligations: Expose stable codes/identifiers and typed event shapes; keep prose for humans only.
Distinguish durable error codes from transient display copy.
Keep credentials, billing URLs and secrets out of machine-readable/log surfaces.
A machine-readable stream reports identity in its first event so a supervisor can persist and reuse it.
Do not change field meaning/order silently; version the contract.

enforcement.implementation: Typed schemas/codes; prose generated separately.
enforcement.trust: Consumers rely on the schema, not messages.
enforcement.failure: An unknown code is surfaced as unknown, not mapped by string matching.
exceptions: A purely interactive human CLI may omit codes if it has no automation contract.

applicability: when: Headless runs, HTTP APIs, event streams, error taxonomies.
exceptions: Internal in-process calls may use typed errors directly.
reactivation: Any consumer script requires the stable contract.

migration.strategy: Add codes/schemas alongside prose; deprecate prose parsing.
migration.implementation: Emit a version, document fields, and test with a real consumer.
migration.requiredSupport: Schema definitions and a stable error taxonomy.

positive: A supervisor parses the id from the first event and resumes the run.
rejection: Changing copy does not change the code.
Credentials never appear in the event/log.
recovery: An unknown code is reported verbatim; no guessed repair is attempted.

limitations: A schema adds maintenance cost.
Some failure detail cannot be reduced to a code; a structured detail field is needed.

mechanisms.title: Separate a policy decision from an execution failure
mechanisms.problem: Treating a denial as an exception, or a failure as a denial, hides the reason, invites retries and can turn a refusal into execution.
triggers: An approval/review gate and an executor both produce outcomes.
A child agent or downstream listener can refuse.
obligations: Model denial/cancellation as a normal, structured outcome distinct from a thrown failure.
On failure, report the actual cause; do not fabricate a policy reason.
Do not retry a denial; retry only transient failures where the contract allows.
A child cannot escalate its own authority; preserve the reason up the chain.
Ask a human only after downstream gates allow, so a later denial/cancel is not laundered into a prompt.

enforcement.implementation: Typed result variants; dispatch checks the allowed variant only. Current source: auto-review returns `kind: 'deny'` under `never`, and only after downstream allows returns `kind: 'ask'` under `ask`; the tools approval seam maps `allowed-once` to allow and `rejected`/`cancelled`/`unavailable` to distinct denials. Target adoption remains planned; source tests were not executed here.
enforcement.trust: The gate owns the decision; the executor owns the failure.
enforcement.failure: Failure is surfaced as failure; denial never executes.
exceptions: An unavailable approver may map to a documented conservative outcome, not to allow.

applicability: when: Approvals, sandbox denials, permission errors, child delegation.
exceptions: A fatal infrastructure error may abort the whole run rather than return a normal denial.
reactivation: Any new gate/result type needs the distinction.

migration.strategy: Replace boolean/exception denials with typed outcomes.
migration.implementation: Add reason codes, UI branches and no-retry rules.
migration.requiredSupport: A result type that can express deny/cancel/fail.

positive: Under approval policy `ask`, a reviewer denial is returned as the tools pipeline's `ask` decision (not an approval-service result); the approval service then maps `allowed-once` to allow and `rejected`, `cancelled`, `unavailable` to deny with distinct reasons, and the body does not run. Under `never`, the reviewer denial is final and no approval prompt occurs.
rejection: A denial is never retried automatically.
A downstream denial prevents an approval prompt.
A reviewer failure denies with a distinct `Auto review of tool "<name>" failed; its body was not executed: <error>` message carrying finish kind, failure code and provider message.
recovery: A transient executor failure may be retried by the caller; a denial is final for that attempt.

limitations: More result variants complicate callers.
Some failures are ambiguous; the contract must choose a default.
The tools pipeline's `ask` decision and the approval service's `ask` policy are different layers; do not report one as the other.

mechanisms.title: Disclose provenance, scope and known limits; do not endorse third-party claims
mechanisms.problem: Presenting a third-party backend, plugin, telemetry default or deferred feature as fully supported hides untested behavior and implied endorsement.
triggers: A capability depends on a third party or an experimental path.
A feature ships with defaults that affect privacy or data.
obligations: Name the exact owner/provider of each capability and what the product actually guarantees.
Do not imply endorsement from inclusion; pin examples/versions and mark them as examples.
Disclose defaults that affect privacy/telemetry and make opt-in/opt-out explicit.
Mark deferred or unverified features as such; do not claim they are implemented.
Separate source-quoted claims from the project's own tested behavior.

An unsigned market index is a set of claims: titles, authors, labels and scores are not DSH verification; clients must show the index URL and each version's source, and the installed manifest/source decides what is installed.

enforcement.implementation: Docs/notes distinguish owned vs external behavior and tested vs planned.
enforcement.trust: None of this is runtime enforcement; it prevents false assurance.
enforcement.failure: An unverified claim is removed or labeled, not silently shipped.
exceptions: A fully owned, tested capability may state a guarantee without third-party caveats.

applicability: when: Backends, plugins, telemetry, experimental/deferred features, external docs.
exceptions: Internal prototypes not exposed to users may omit user-facing disclosure.
reactivation: Any new dependency or default needs a disclosure pass.

migration.strategy: Add provenance/limits sections and pin examples.
migration.implementation: Review claims against tests; label planned work.
migration.requiredSupport: Accurate ownership metadata.

positive: Third-party MCP examples are pinned and labeled as interoperability examples, not endorsement; backend notes state provider-specific tested scope.
An unsigned market index is presented with its index URL and each version's source; an `official` label is not treated as DSH verification.
rejection: A deferred feature is not described as available.
Shared-base telemetry with unset/empty `DSH_TELEMETRY_MODE` resolves to `FEEDBACK_ONLY`; no upload occurs without explicit feedback.
Plugin omitted `mode` resolves to `DISABLED`; non-empty `DSH_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` is a hard opt-out; `FULL` is rejected.
recovery: A proposed desktop update extension remains labeled proposed and is not an initial acceptance requirement; an untested claim is labeled rather than presented as implemented.

limitations: Documentation can drift from code.
Inclusion still signals some approval; the disclosure must be prominent.

mechanisms.title: Versioned formats validate recognized fields strictly; tolerate unknown members only where the contract grants it
mechanisms.problem: A permissive reader that accepts typos or invalid values in fields the format defines turns producer bugs into silent behavior; an unversioned format cannot evolve. A blanket closed-schema rule is equally wrong: some formats explicitly promise forward compatibility and require readers to ignore members they do not define.
triggers: A file/JSON/event schema is exchanged between components or ecosystems.
A consumer must tolerate future producers.
obligations: Version the format and validate every defined field, value and discriminator strictly; reject defined-rule violations and unknown closed discriminator values (for example an unknown `source.type`).
Do not infer semantics from unknown members; ignore members the format does not define only where that format's contract explicitly grants forward compatibility.
Require exactly one representation for a concept; do not accept both optional aliases.
Reuse maintained parsers/validators for standard names/versions where possible.
Separate format definition from generation; a generator may change without changing the format.
A change existing readers would misinterpret requires a new format version; optional additions that readers can ignore do not.
Record the per-format tolerance decision instead of applying one global closed/open rule.
steps: Test unknown fields and version mismatch.

enforcement.implementation: Per-format validator at the boundary: strict defined-field checks plus an explicit unknown-member policy.
enforcement.trust: The format contract states tolerance; no consumer-side guessing.
enforcement.failure: A defined-rule violation fails with a diagnostic; an unknown member is ignored only under an explicit forward-compatibility rule, otherwise it is rejected.
exceptions: The web diff card returns the generic path for an unknown `card` value instead of guessing a diff.
The plugin-market reader ignores members the note does not define at every level while rejecting an unknown `source.type`.

applicability: when: Configs, plugin indexes, event streams, message formats.
exceptions: Free-form user content is not schema-validated.
reactivation: Any new exchanged format needs a version and strictness decision.

migration.strategy: Keep or add a format version; validate defined fields strictly and record the unknown-member policy per format.
migration.implementation: Replace blanket unknown-field rejection with per-format rules; test defined-field violations, unknown discriminator values, and ignorable optional members.
migration.requiredSupport: A schema validator and a documented compatibility policy per format.

positive: A current-version plugin-market index with valid defined fields parses; members the note does not define are dropped at every level.
A web diff card with an unknown `card` value renders the generic path, not a partial diff.
rejection: A plugin-market index with an undeclared category/label/sort key, an unlisted dist-tag target, a duplicate name/version, or `format` other than 1 fails the whole index with a JSON-path diagnostic.
An unknown `source.type` is rejected; a typo in a defined field is not ignored.
recovery: A change existing readers would misinterpret uses a new `format` value; an old reader reports the unsupported format rather than partially parsing.
An optional member added to format 1 is ignored by an existing reader and does not require a new version.

limitations: Tolerance rules differ by format; a single cross-format closed-schema rule would reject the plugin-market reader's forward-compatibility contract.
Ignoring unknown members weakens typo detection in formats that grant it.

mechanisms.title: Previews read; they never mutate the draft, source or activation state
mechanisms.problem: A preview that serializes the draft, submits it, fetches remote content on render or changes activation couples inspection to side effects.
triggers: A UI offers hover/click preview of a file, skill, plan or remote resource.
The preview shares state with an editable composer.
obligations: Clicking/hovering a preview must not serialize, submit or mutate the draft.
Preview data is transient discovery data; it is not added to durable messages or state.
Source-owned activation resolves the reference; the composer does not implement provider policy.
Do not load full skill bodies/remote content during discovery; fetch only on explicit preview.
A preview may be unavailable; show that state without substituting content.
steps: Route the reference to its source owner.
Test unchanged draft and no submit.

enforcement.implementation: Read-only preview path; separate activation/serialization.
enforcement.trust: The source owner resolves; the composer only displays.
enforcement.failure: An invalid reference shows invalid; no draft mutation.
exceptions: An explicit insert action is a separate command, not a preview.

applicability: when: Composer references, file hovers, skill previews, plan inspection.
exceptions: A preview pane that intentionally edits a copy must state that it is an editor.
reactivation: Any new preview gesture needs the no-side-effect rule.

migration.strategy: Split preview from insertion and move resolution to the source owner.
migration.implementation: Add transient metadata, lazy fetch, invalidation, and draft-unchanged tests.
migration.requiredSupport: Source-owned reference resolution.

positive: Clicking a file chip previews it and leaves the draft byte-identical.
rejection: Preview never submits or serializes the message.
Discovery does not load skill bodies.
recovery: An uncached preview awaits the catalog; an invalidated reference is removed without touching the draft.

limitations: Lazy previews can be slow on first click.
Transient preview data can be confused with durable content if not labeled.

mechanisms.title: Make required facts required; exactly one representation
mechanisms.problem: Optional fields let a producer omit a fact the consumer needs, then a default silently invents it; two optional aliases force downstream branching.
triggers: A schema or tool input has a fact that must always hold.
Two fields can express the same concept.
obligations: Mark required facts required and fail when they are absent; do not substitute a default.
Represent one concept with exactly one field/shape; do not accept both query and queries, or both a boolean and a count.
Validation errors name the missing field; they are not swallowed into a generic failure.
A display-only value may be optional only if every consumer can render its absence explicitly.
Adoption guidance (not source-derived): adding a required field to an existing format needs a version/compatibility plan.
steps: Make them required in the schema.

enforcement.implementation: Required validation at the boundary; no fallback default.
enforcement.trust: The schema is the contract.
enforcement.failure: Missing required value fails with a diagnostic; execution does not proceed.
exceptions: Backward-compatible optional additions may be allowed if absence is meaningful.

applicability: when: Tool schemas, APIs, configs, manifests.
exceptions: Free-form metadata may be optional.
reactivation: Any new required fact needs schema enforcement.

migration.strategy: Tighten schemas and migrate producers.
migration.implementation: Replace optional/aliases, add diagnostics, test old payloads.
migration.requiredSupport: Schema versioning and a producer update.

positive: A complete payload validates and executes.
rejection: Missing required fields and both-alias payloads are rejected before side effects.
recovery: A producer updated to the new schema succeeds; no consumer-side default is applied.

limitations: Strict required fields break old clients; a staged rollout is needed.

mechanisms.title: Bound every read, fan-out and displayed payload
mechanisms.problem: An unbounded read, query fan-out or preview can consume memory/latency proportional to an untrusted corpus and hang the caller.
triggers: A tool reads a file, index, search corpus, directory tree or plugin list.
A model can choose an array size or depth.
obligations: Apply an explicit deployment-owned cap to entries, lines, bytes, pages and fan-out.
A cap must be visible in the tool description/prompt so the model can plan.
On cap overflow, return a bounded result with an explicit truncation marker, not a silently partial one.
Stream or page large content; do not materialize an unbounded body.
A preview cap and a reading cap may differ, but both are explicit constants.

Enforce a fixed-rate floor as one protocol constant: `MIN_EVERY_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 60` is read by the Host decoder, create/update validation and the tool description; the client keeps its own `MIN_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 60`, and a deployment cannot raise the protocol floor through configuration.

enforcement.implementation: Hard caps in the tool/service; bounded preview components.
enforcement.trust: The service enforces; callers cannot opt into unbounded.
enforcement.failure: Oversized input is rejected or truncated with a marker.
exceptions: An internal trusted pipeline may use a larger bound if it is still finite.

applicability: when: File reads, directory listings, search, plugin indexes, previews.
exceptions: A local single-user tool may use a high bound but must not be infinite.
reactivation: Any new corpus-facing read needs a bound.

migration.strategy: Add configurable caps and truncation metadata.
migration.implementation: Enforce server-side, document defaults, test at the cap and above.
migration.requiredSupport: Config plumbing and bounded data structures.

positive: A query within the cap returns complete results; an oversized array is rejected before fan-out.

A fixed-rate interval below 60 seconds is rejected by the Host decoder/create/update; `MIN_EVERY_INTERVAL_SECONDS = 60` is shared, and a deployment cannot raise the protocol floor through configuration.
rejection: No request can cause an unbounded number of provider calls.
recovery: A truncated preview offers an explicit expand path; the underlying read remains bounded.

limitations: Caps can hide data the user wanted; the marker must be clear.
Choosing a cap is deployment-specific.
A deployment that needs a longer fixed-rate minimum must enforce it in the creating interface, not by raising the protocol constant.

mechanisms.title: Bounded reconnect/retry with one outage budget and quiescent disposal
mechanisms.problem: Unbounded reconnect storms, retry counters that reset on brief success, or disposal that only signals stop leave a resource flapping or leaking after the owner is gone.
triggers: A remote connection, provider fetch or runtime download can fail transiently.
An owner can be disposed while an attempt is in flight.
obligations: Use exponential backoff bounded by max delay and a single outage budget of consecutive failed attempts.
Do not reset the budget on a briefly successful connect; only a stable recovery resets it.
One queue serializes operations; each attempt uses a fresh transport/client generation.
On budget exhaustion, unregister/disable the resource and stop; do not loop forever.
Disposal flips a fence, cancels timers, closes the client, then awaits in-flight attempts and queues before releasing.
Fallback to a smaller/local form must be explicit; a failed remote must not fabricate success.
steps: Detect failure via events, not polling.

enforcement.implementation: Supervisor with generations, bounded backoff, outage budget, disposal fence.
enforcement.trust: The supervisor owns health; callers do not retry unbounded.
enforcement.failure: Exhaustion disables/unregisters and logs; disposal awaits quiescence.
exceptions: A transport with its own reconnect (HTTP SSE) may be left to that owner.

applicability: when: MCP connections, remote providers, downloads, streaming transports.
exceptions: A one-shot request with no persistent resource may simply fail.
reactivation: Any long-lived connection needs bounded recovery and disposal.

migration.strategy: Add a supervisor with bounded policy and quiescent teardown.
migration.implementation: Serialize syncs, use generations, expose states, test crash loops and dispose races.
migration.requiredSupport: Config schema for backoff and a cancellable timer.

positive: A crashed stdio server is retried with delays doubling from `initialDelayMs` to `maxDelayMs`; one outage consumes at most `maxAttempts` consecutive failures.
rejection: A crash loop exhausts the budget and stops instead of resetting on brief connects.
A late attempt after disposal cannot register tools.
recovery: Budget resets only after stable recovery; fallback content is marked as fallback.

limitations: Backoff delays recovery for a transient blip.
A permanently disabled server needs user action.

mechanisms.title: Multi-item operations are all-or-nothing and fan out only within a bound
mechanisms.problem: Returning partial success for a batched request lets callers believe all items completed, while unbounded fan-out multiplies cost and failure.
triggers: One call accepts an array of queries/items.
The operation can be parallelized across a provider.
obligations: If any item fails, discard successful siblings and return the failure; do not claim partial success unless the contract explicitly supports per-item results.
Wait for sibling cancellation to reach quiescence before returning.
Bound the array and the fan-out with one deployment-owned cap.
Keep the shared provider contract single-item; orchestration belongs in the consumer.
Deduplicate/label results by originating item so a combined result remains attributable.
steps: Join; on failure cancel siblings and discard.
