enforcement.implementation: Consumer-level orchestration with all-or-nothing join and bounded concurrency.
enforcement.trust: The consumer owns the batch semantics; providers stay simple.
enforcement.failure: Any failure fails the call; siblings are cancelled and awaited.
exceptions: A contract that explicitly returns per-item outcomes may preserve successes, but must label them.

applicability: when: Search queries, bulk mutations, batch fetches.
exceptions: Idempotent independent items may be retried individually by the caller.
reactivation: Any array input needs a batch semantics decision.

migration.strategy: Move orchestration into the consumer and define all-or-nothing.
migration.implementation: Add cap, cancellation quiescence, labeling, and tests for one failing item.
migration.requiredSupport: A concurrent search/mutation API.

positive: A batch within the cap returns combined labeled results.
rejection: One failed item fails the whole call and no success is reported.
An array over the cap is rejected before provider calls.
recovery: Sibling cancellation is awaited; a retry starts a fresh batch.

limitations: All-or-nothing wastes successful work on one failure.
Fan-out bound may underuse available capacity.

mechanisms.title: Record supersession lineage and preserve prior decisions
mechanisms.problem: A new note or decision silently replaces an earlier one; readers cannot tell which parts still hold, and old constraints vanish without an audit trail.
triggers: A design changes an earlier decision.
A note is archived or superseded.
obligations: Name the predecessor and state exactly which facts are superseded and which still hold.
Keep the predecessor readable; archive rather than rewrite history.
An update block records what later removed or changed a mechanism.
Do not silently rename a concept to avoid the lineage; migration notes are part of the change.
The current authority is the latest explicit decision, not an unmarked old note.

enforcement.implementation: Note templates carry status/update/supersedes fields.
enforcement.trust: Documentation discipline, not runtime.
enforcement.failure: An unreferenced contradiction is a review defect; the newer note is not automatically authoritative without the block.
exceptions: A purely additive note may have no predecessor.

applicability: when: Agent Notes, ADRs, policy changes, migrations.
exceptions: A brand-new area with no prior decision.
reactivation: Any change to an existing decision needs lineage.

migration.strategy: Add lineage blocks and link predecessors.
migration.implementation: Update templates; audit archived notes for unmarked supersession.
migration.requiredSupport: Stable note paths and a searchable archive.

positive: The background-job completion note names its predecessor and states that it supersedes exactly the fact that completion never wakes an idle owner while keeping every other task-runtime decision.
The ACP note's line-9 blockquote records that it was written when ACP was an editor bridge and that the automation-only protocol removal left the multiplexing decision unchanged.
rejection: A note that contradicts a predecessor without naming it is returned for revision; an update/supersedes block must name the predecessor and the fact it supersedes.
recovery: A later note can restore a superseded fact explicitly, again with lineage.

limitations: Lineage depends on author honesty.
Long chains are hard to read; the current note must summarize.

mechanisms.title: Gate risky features behind one explicit, documented switch; the default is owner-decided
mechanisms.problem: Experimental, privacy-affecting or complexity-adding features need one explicit, documented gate and a documented current default. A name prefix is not a gate, and a falsy env value must not enable an experimental command. Default-off cannot be assumed: developer tools moved from an initial default-off choice to a default-on decision, and the shared telemetry base defaults to FEEDBACK_ONLY, not DISABLED.
triggers: A feature is unproven, privacy-sensitive or disrupts routine work.
A CLI/subcommand or UI surface can be toggled.
obligations: Choose one explicit gate per feature and document its current default; do not infer the default from the mechanism name or from a superseded note.
For an experimental command, require a per-invocation `--experimental` flag or `DSH_EXPERIMENTAL=1`; `1` is the only enabling value, and a bare command fails with exit 1 naming both opt-ins.

For the developer-tools preference, resolve the accepted `ui-settings.enabled` value; the initial default-off was explicitly superseded by the default-on decision (`ui-developer-tools.enabled` schema default `true`), while a saved `false` wins.
For telemetry, preserve both defaults: shared base unset/empty `DSH_TELEMETRY_MODE` -> `FEEDBACK_ONLY`; plugin omitted `mode` -> `DISABLED`; non-empty `DSH_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` is the hard opt-out.
Gate on one owner; do not read process.env deep inside pure parsing.
Turning off hides/removes active content (remount), not just the control.
Stabilizing means deleting the gate, not renaming the command; preserve the historical superseded default explicitly rather than erasing it.
steps: Choose the gate owner and record the current default.
Check the gate before side effects.
Test bare, false, true and saved-preference paths.
Apply the shared setting to every surface that renders the feature.
Delete the gate on stabilization without renaming the command; keep predecessor links.

enforcement.implementation: Flag/env check for experimental commands; settings-owned developerTools preference; telemetry mode resolution at the base/plugin boundary.
enforcement.trust: The gate is explicit and documented, not a security boundary for untrusted users.
enforcement.failure: A bare experimental command or false value fails; a stored developer-tools `false` withholds capabilities; telemetry `FULL` is rejected and non-empty `DSH_TELEMETRY_DISABLED` opts out.
exceptions: A feature required for the product to function cannot be gated off.
A safe diagnostic may default on if documented.

applicability: when: Experimental commands, telemetry, developer tools, previews.
exceptions: A safe diagnostic that cannot affect data may default on if documented.
reactivation: Any new risky feature needs an explicit gate with a documented owner-decided default.

migration.strategy: Introduce one documented gate per feature and record the owner-decided default; preserve superseded defaults explicitly.
migration.implementation: Check before side effects; test bare/false/true/saved-preference paths; apply shared settings; keep predecessor links.
migration.requiredSupport: Config/env parsing, a settings form, and a note template that records supersession.

positive: `dsh meta --experimental` and `DSH_EXPERIMENTAL=1 dsh meta` run; `DSH_EXPERIMENTAL=0` and the bare command fail with exit 1 naming both opt-ins.

The `ui-developer-tools.enabled` Host schema defaults to `true`; after preference resolution the accepted `ui-settings.enabled` value is `true`; a saved `false` still withholds developer tools; the initial default-off note is preserved as superseded, not erased.
Unset/empty `DSH_TELEMETRY_MODE` resolves to `FEEDBACK_ONLY`; omitted plugin `mode` resolves to `DISABLED`; `FULL` is rejected.
rejection: A falsy env value (`0`, `false`, empty) does not enable an experimental command; only `1` does.
A stored developer-tools `false` does not render scripted HTML/iframe content; turning off remounts/hides active content.
A telemetry configuration that treats FEEDBACK_ONLY as DISABLED, or claims universal default-off, fails this mechanism.
recovery: Removing the gate on stabilization leaves the command name unchanged; a superseded default remains readable in its predecessor note.

limitations: Env gating complicates reproducible scripts.
Users may set a global env and forget.

Defaults differ by owner: experimental commands are off, developer tools are on after preference resolution, and telemetry is FEEDBACK_ONLY at the base but DISABLED when the plugin mode is omitted; one blanket default-off rule is wrong.

mechanisms.title: Share one presentation base and token set across surfaces
mechanisms.problem: Desktop and Web each define their own defaults, focus colors or geometry, so the same feature looks and behaves differently and fixes must be duplicated.
triggers: Several renderers/surfaces present the same concept.
A design token (focus, radius, width) is introduced.
obligations: Define one shared base/default and derive surface-specific choices from it.
Use one token per role (for example one keyboard-focus colour for every control) rather than per-component values.
A shared setting/preference applies to every surface that renders the feature; do not scope it to one host.
Deviations are explicit exceptions with a reason, not independent defaults.
Adoption guidance (not source-derived): string/copy defaults live in the shared i18n seat, not in each surface.

enforcement.implementation: Shared tokens/base module imported by all surfaces.
enforcement.trust: None; consistency is structural.
enforcement.failure: A surface without the shared base is a review defect.
exceptions: Platform constraints (for example native focus) may require a documented override.

applicability: when: Web/Desktop/TUI/mobile surfaces sharing a feature.
exceptions: A platform-only control may have no counterpart.
reactivation: Any second renderer needs the shared base.

migration.strategy: Extract tokens/base and replace local values.
migration.implementation: One PR per surface, parity tests, delete duplicates.
migration.requiredSupport: A shared UI package.

positive: The model-input control renders one shared row with one shared default; a surface does not introduce a private selector default.
Every control reads the `--dsw-focus-ring-color` token; the focus stylesheet owns one colour and one standard 2px width, with dense tables/toolbars allowed 1px.
One settings-owned `ThemeSettingsSchema.fontSize` value (12–17, default 14) feeds the transcript and composer through `--dsh-content-font-size`.
rejection: A surface that defines a private default for a shared role (model input, focus colour, font size) fails this mechanism.
A component-local focus colour instead of `--dsw-focus-ring-color`, or a private font-size default, is rejected.
recovery: A token change propagates to all consumers on rebuild; a mapped settings value survives reload and applies live.

limitations: Shared packages can become a dumping ground.
Platform differences still need exceptions.

mechanisms.title: Enforce at the narrowest owner and keep scope explicit
mechanisms.problem: A control that hides UI without changing the underlying capability leaves active content running; a policy applied globally can break unrelated surfaces.
triggers: A feature toggle, sandbox or permission affects only part of the system.
Disabling a view must also stop its side effects.
obligations: Enforce at the owner of the capability (renderer, sandbox, provider), not only at the control.
Turning off must dispose/remount active content, not just hide a button.
Scope a setting/policy to the surfaces it actually governs; state the scope.
A per-session privacy/telemetry choice applies to that session; do not leak it to others.
A sandbox/permission mode names exactly what it allows and what it denies.

enforcement.implementation: Owner-level checks/disposal; scoped config.
enforcement.trust: The owner enforces; the UI is not the boundary.
enforcement.failure: Off means no capability; active instances are torn down.
exceptions: A cosmetic toggle may only hide if it has no side effects.

applicability: when: Developer tools, HTML preview, telemetry, sandbox modes.
exceptions: Pure display toggles with no capability.
reactivation: Any new toggle needs a side-effect analysis.

migration.strategy: Move enforcement to the owner and dispose on disable.
migration.implementation: Add remount/dispose logic, scope docs, tests for active content.
migration.requiredSupport: Lifecycle hooks in the renderer/sandbox.

positive: Disabling developer tools removes the active View/tab bar and disposes the iframe.
rejection: A hidden but still-running script is a defect.
A session-scoped telemetry choice does not affect another session.
recovery: Re-enabling reconstructs from current settings; no stale active content survives.

limitations: Disposal can lose unsaved preview state.
Scoping adds configuration surface.

mechanisms.title: One shared base default when no surface overrides
mechanisms.problem: Several compositions each define a fallback, so a new surface silently behaves differently and a fix must be applied repeatedly.
triggers: A capability has a default that most compositions share.
Multiple deployment compositions exist.
obligations: Put the default in one shared base composition/layer; surface compositions override only explicitly.
Do not duplicate the default in each composition; a missing override uses the base.
Name the precedence: surface > base > absent.
A change to the shared default is visible to all consumers; test at least one override and one inherited case.

enforcement.implementation: Composition merge with one base default.
enforcement.trust: The loader owns precedence.
enforcement.failure: An absent override falls back to base; a conflicting duplicate is removed.
exceptions: A composition that must not have the capability explicitly removes it.

applicability: when: Plugin compositions, default search/fetch, feature defaults.
exceptions: A one-off deployment may override with a documented reason.
reactivation: Any second composition needs the base.

migration.strategy: Move defaults into the shared base and delete local copies.
migration.implementation: Update compositions, document precedence, test inherited behavior.
migration.requiredSupport: A composition/merge system.

positive: A composition without an override gets the shared default.
rejection: A duplicate local default is removed in review.
recovery: Reverting an override restores the base default.

limitations: A shared default can surprise a surface that wanted absence.
Merge precedence must be documented.

mechanisms.title: Use the maintained protocol owner; do not fork or reimplement negotiation
mechanisms.problem: Hand-rolled protocol negotiation or a forked SDK drifts from the standard, misses capabilities and multiplies maintenance.
triggers: A client connects to an external protocol/server.
A version/capability handshake exists.
obligations: Delegate connection, negotiation and transport lifecycle to the maintained SDK/library.
Keep the harness's own seam thin: config resolution, lifecycle, policy.
Do not reimplement version negotiation from scratch when the owner provides it.
A connection generation uses one protocol instance; do not reuse across transports.
Report unsupported capabilities explicitly rather than pretending.
steps: Test negotiation against a real server.

enforcement.implementation: Current source: SDK Client inside the connection supervisor with versionNegotiation { mode: 'auto' }; bridge calls high-level listTools/callTool and has no parallel protocol code. The archived note says client 2.0.0; the fixed-commit manifest pins @modelcontextprotocol/client 2.2.0. Target adoption remains planned; source tests were not executed here.
enforcement.trust: The SDK owns the wire; the harness owns lifecycle.
enforcement.failure: Negotiation failure is reported; no fallback protocol guess.
exceptions: A protocol with no maintained client may require a first-party implementation, which then becomes the owner.

applicability: when: MCP, LSP, DAP, provider SDKs.
exceptions: A tiny stable protocol may be implemented directly if fully specified and tested.
reactivation: Any new external protocol needs an owner decision.

migration.strategy: Replace hand-rolled negotiation with the SDK; keep a thin supervisor.
migration.implementation: Delete parallel code, add real-server tests.
migration.requiredSupport: The maintained library.

positive: `@deepseek-ai/dsh-mcp-client` declares `@modelcontextprotocol/client` 2.2.0 and constructs `new Client(..., { versionNegotiation: { mode: 'auto' } })`; discovery calls high-level `client.listTools(undefined, { cacheMode: 'refresh' })`, and each registered tool delegates to `client.callTool(..., { toolDefinition: tool })`; the bridge adds no parallel pagination code.
rejection: Unsupported capabilities are reported, not emulated.
No second wire implementation exists.
recovery: A failed negotiation surfaces an error; reconnect starts a fresh generation.

limitations: SDK bugs become yours to work around.
SDK version upgrades can be breaking; the archived note names client 2.0.0 while the fixed-commit manifest pins 2.2.0.
The no-parallel-pagination claim concerns tools discovery; the bridge also exposes SDK resource methods, which receive and return the SDK cursor unchanged rather than iterating it.

mechanisms.title: Diagnostics observe without taking ownership or mutating state
mechanisms.problem: An inspector that subscribes as an owner, writes to the log or replays with side effects changes the system it is measuring.
triggers: A debug/inspector/trace view reads live state.
A diagnostic tool needs history.
obligations: Diagnostic views are read-only: no writes to the observed log/state, no ownership acquisition, no replay with side effects.
Use weak/lazy references and bounded reads so inspection does not keep resources alive.
A diagnostic fact must be labeled with its source and scope; do not present a partial view as complete.
Cancelling/closing the inspector does not cancel the observed work unless explicitly requested.
A diagnostic path must not become a second rendering/derivation authority.

enforcement.implementation: Read-only APIs; no write handles; lazy references. The source's read-only Session Inspector (existing loaded window and pagination, only the selected table subscribes) is distinct from the opt-in inspector-profile bundle that adds the debugging Worker and fetch capture.
enforcement.trust: The inspector is outside the authority path.
enforcement.failure: A failed read shows unavailable; it does not repair or write.
exceptions: The default-off `inspector-profile` optional bundle is a separate privileged capability, not part of the diagnostic-read contract: its patch enables the Inspector with `captureFetch: true`, starting the NodeJS Inspector with local code execution and unredacted Host fetch capture (complete URL, headers, request/response bodies, status, timing, errors, cancellation); closing the debugging window does not stop capture. Redaction is an adoption requirement, not source behavior.

applicability: when: Session inspector, trajectory, diagnostics, trace viewers.
exceptions: A repair tool is not a diagnostic read and must be labeled.
reactivation: Any new inspector needs the read-only contract.

migration.strategy: Separate read APIs from write/ownership; add bounded lazy reads.
migration.implementation: Remove write handles, add scope labels, test no-side-effect.
migration.requiredSupport: A read-only projection of the log.

positive: The Session Inspector registers no resource provider, Conversation header slot, composer, or product navigation API; Session Controller and Chat retain data ownership; only the selected table subscribes; the log uses the existing loaded window and pagination.
rejection: Opening/closing the default Inspector does not change ownership or run state.

Treating the read-only contract as covering the debugging bundle fails: enabling `inspector-profile` activates `captureFetch: true`, the NodeJS Inspector with local code execution, and unredacted Host fetch capture without a debugging argument; closing the debugging window does not stop capture.
recovery: A missing/partial record shows unavailable; no reconstruction write occurs.

limitations: Read-only views may lag live state.

The opt-in `inspector-profile` bundle is a separate privileged capability, not a property of the read-only Inspector: it permits local code execution and unredacted Host fetch capture; it does not redact credentials, cookies, query values or payloads. A deployment must add redaction; the source does not.

mechanisms.title: One flow owns disclosure state and key semantics
mechanisms.problem: Letting each child own its own disclosure/keyboard state loses it when a parent unmounts, and duplicated key handling makes Escape/Enter behave differently across surfaces.
triggers: A flow has nested phases, disclosures or selection surfaces.
Several surfaces share keyboard conventions.
obligations: Keep one owner for the flow's disclosure state, with a per-phase map that survives parent hide/restore.
Preserve the user's choice across ordinary updates; open only on a defined transition (clean→activity) and close on a defined completion.
Mirror the primary flow's keys consistently (for example Enter/Tab settle, Escape/Shift+Tab dismiss) across selection surfaces.
A user-dismissed hit stays dismissed for the same token/query until it changes.
Focus-aware completion: do not close content while focus is inside it.
Do not add a second store/setting/timer for the same flow.
steps: Own state at the flow root.
Key child state by stable phase key.

enforcement.implementation: Root-owned state map; shared key handling.
enforcement.trust: The flow owner is the single authority.
enforcement.failure: A child unmount does not discard state; an unknown key does nothing.
exceptions: A standalone surface without a parent flow owns its own state.

applicability: when: Workflow runs, background jobs, composer selection, disclosure panels.
exceptions: A trivial one-level disclosure may keep local state.
reactivation: Any nested flow needs an owner.

migration.strategy: Lift state to the flow owner and share key semantics.
migration.implementation: Add phase map, transition rules, dismissal identity, focus checks.
migration.requiredSupport: A stable phase key and keyboard event router.

positive: Hiding and reopening the outer flow restores each phase choice.
rejection: An ordinary running update does not override a user's collapsed choice.
A dismissed hit does not reopen on the same query.
recovery: A remount reconstructs state from current durable status; a removed phase drops its entry.

limitations: Root-owned state grows with phases.
Key semantics must match each platform's expectations.

mechanisms.title: Rewrite promoted third-party features as first-party code
mechanisms.problem: Vendoring a community plugin keeps its untested JavaScript, external version gates and foreign ownership; exempting it creates a second package class.
triggers: A community/third-party feature is promoted into the product.
A plugin carries its own release/version compatibility gate.
obligations: Rewrite the feature in the repository's own packages, following its typecheck, coverage, i18n and invariant gates.
Split ownership along existing host/client package seams; reuse shared utilities rather than vendoring lib/.
Delete external-version compatibility gates; a first-party package is versioned with the repository.
Keep the trust fence (origin/auth) around every new route.
Use the shared snapshot store for persisted choices; do not hand-roll storage.
A first-party rewrite must not preserve a parallel plugin path.
steps: Remove the external gate and plugin dependency.
Apply standard gates and trust fences.

enforcement.implementation: First-party packages with standard checks; no exemption class.
enforcement.trust: The platform's trust fence and review gates, not the plugin's.
enforcement.failure: A vendored lib that fails gates is rejected; the plugin path is removed.
exceptions: A genuinely external integration may remain a plugin if it cannot be owned, but must be labeled.

applicability: when: Promoting a community plugin or vendored feature.
exceptions: A thin adapter to a maintained third-party SDK may remain, owned by the adapter.
reactivation: Any new promotion repeats the rewrite.

migration.strategy: Rewrite rather than vendor; delete the plugin and its gates.
migration.implementation: Create host/client packages, reuse primitives, add trust fence, run standard gates.
migration.requiredSupport: Existing package seams and shared utilities.

positive: The feature passes typecheck, coverage, i18n and invariant gates as a first-party package.
rejection: A vendored lib/ with an exemption is rejected.
The external DSH-version gate no longer exists.
recovery: If the rewrite regresses, the old plugin is not kept as a silent fallback; the defect is fixed in the owned code.

limitations: Rewrite cost is real.
A community feature may depend on external services the product cannot own.

mechanisms.title: Choose the completion delivery lane from owner state
mechanisms.problem: Completion delivered only by injection never reaches an idle owner; waking unconditionally can launder a user interrupt into a new turn and create a self-exciting wake chain.
triggers: A background job, subagent or terminal completes while its owner may be busy, idle or cancelled.
A completion is delivered as a new turn or injected message.
obligations: Select the lane from owner state: a busy owner is injected; an idle owner is woken with followup; no busy-polling or sleeping.
A cancelled turn is a user interrupt; never reopen it on the user behalf.
Waking is unbounded by default; an opt-in cap counts owner turns, not time; claiming a user-authored message restores the budget.
A quiet mode may restore the old injection lane for deterministic transcripts; it is explicit, not the default.
Delivery is a correctness rule with one owner; completion is not a mere notification.
The registry/ledger may move; the lane rule does not change with the implementation.
steps: Classify owner state from the live driver; only an idle owner is a wake candidate.
Inject for a busy or cancelled-converging owner; call followup for an idle owner under wakeup.
Suppress settlements that are awaited, model-killed, teardown or unowned.
Apply an optional per-owner turn-count cap; refill it only when user-authored input is claimed.
Use quiet explicitly for deterministic transcripts.

enforcement.implementation: Current source: @deepseek-ai/dsh-tool-jobs owns delivery. Its settlement subscription ({ owners: 'scope' }) skips event.awaited, model-killed jobs, unowned jobs and teardown settlements; a wakeup delivery calls followup() only when owner.status === 'idle', otherwise inject(). maxConsecutiveWakes is counted per exact Agent in a WeakMap and reset only by agent/inbox/claimed with message.source.kind === 'user'. The old registry reported bit/onJobDone no longer owns delivery. Target adoption remains planned and source tests were not executed here.
enforcement.trust: The session driver owns turn state; the job registry cannot force a new turn.
enforcement.failure: A cancelled owner is not woken; cap exhaustion degrades to injection and waits for the next turn.
exceptions: Quiet mode intentionally degrades to injection for deterministic transcripts.

applicability: when: Background/continuable work, subagents, terminals, any asynchronous completion delivered to an agent owner.
exceptions: A one-shot foreground call has no completion lane.; A deliberately quiet mode may suppress wakeup.
reactivation: Any completions that can outlive the owner turn need a lane decision.

migration.strategy: Keep the lane decision in the component that owns completion delivery; use the job registry for routing/settlement facts, not for forcing a turn.
migration.implementation: Add a busy/idle branch, teardown/awaited/model-kill suppression, an optional per-owner turn cap refilled only on human input, and an explicit quiet mode; test wake of an idle owner and non-wake of a cancelled-converging owner.
migration.requiredSupport: A session driver exposing live owner status and a followup wake primitive, plus a settlement subscription that distinguishes awaited, killed, teardown and unowned work.

positive: An idle owner is woken and continues; a busy owner receives injection without a new turn; under quiet the idle owner stays on injection.
An awaited settlement, a job killed through job_kill, a teardown settlement and an unowned job each produce no notice; another mounted preset cannot deliver across its scope.
rejection: A cancelled-converging owner is not reopened; a completion cannot busy-poll the owner.
A plugin-queued notice does not refill the wake budget; only a claimed user-authored message does.
recovery: Cap exhaustion degrades to injection until the next turn; a user-authored claim restores the budget; quiet mode is explicit.

limitations: Waking creates turns and can be self-exciting; the cap is opt-in and a spent budget is not restored by time.
Quiet mode trades immediacy for deterministic transcripts, and a notice past the cap waits silently.
